body.text: Beaconsfield mine collapse survivor Todd Russell has died at the age of 54 after an undisclosed illness, his family has confirmed.
Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff posted this morning: "Vale Todd Russell. Thoughts this morning are with Todd's loved ones and everyone who had the absolute pleasure of knowing him."

Last week, Russell posted to social media that, after eight and a half months in hospital, he was returning home to see out his final days surrounded by family. His family has not disclosed his illness.
Russell was one of two Tasmanian miners thrown into the world spotlight after becoming trapped by a rockfall on Anzac Day 2006.
He and co-worker Brant Webb were presumed dead after the body of a third miner, Larry Knight, was found amongst the rubble, nearly a kilometre underground.
But the pair were discovered alive, trapped in the basket of the vehicle they had been working in — a space about the size of a dinner table.

"We had how many tonnes of rock suspended above us like a jigsaw puzzle and we only needed one rock to move for it to come crushing in, killing Brant and myself," Russell told ABC podcast I Was Actually There in 2024.
Initially, Russell could only move his forearms and his head: "Everything else was completely buried," he told the ABC.
"You can imagine the bone bruising from the rocks that landed on top of us."

The pair survived on a single muesli bar and groundwater that seeped through the nearby rocks for the five days it took before rescuers, who had been blasting a new tunnel to reach them, made contact.
As Australia's TV news crews joined the growing scrum around the Beaconsfield mine tower in April 2006, work went on underground to save Russell and Webb.
Australia and the world were captivated, and then on May 9, the pair emerged not only to cheers, but to their lives forever changed.
"It was just a constant barrage of media frenzy for days on end," Russell told the podcast.
"Like reporters hanging over your fence when you're trying to have a cup of tea and a bit of toast for breakfast.
"It was constant, not only for the first few days, but probably for the first 18 months.
"I hated it because you went to work as a normal person, and you come out of there with your identity lost. And people felt that they knew you because they'd been watching you for 14 days."
There was a book about the mine collapse within months of the pair's rescue.
The following year, rock band The Foo Fighters released a song called 'Ballad of the Beaconsfield Miners'.
A telemovie, Beaconsfield, was released to mark the sixth anniversary of the pair's rescue.
Behind all of this was a man struggling with mental ill health, exacerbated by the loss of his parents in the years after his rescue.
He told the podcast he came home one day to find his wife and kids packed and in the car, ready to leave him.
"There was only one person that couldn't see the direction that I was heading, and that was myself,"
he said.
Russell sought professional help to deal with his experience inside the collapsed mine — and the aftermath of the event.
He told the podcast that in 2024 he had been working on rebuilding his relationships and that he had become a proud grandfather.
Russell did not venture into a mining career until he was in his late 20s.
Above ground, he was a keen footballer and hunter, and later, he became part of the Beaconsfield Fire Brigade, retiring as its chief in 2026.
But publicly, he was best known for the famous mine rescue.
In 2022, he told sports podcast The Friday Frothy he saw himself in two ways:
"There's Popeye, who's a big, tough man. But there's Tweety Bird. Behind the scenes, a lot of people don't see when I go and sit and cry.
"I put on a tough exterior when I'm out in public and stuff, and they think, 'Oh, he's going alright,' but they don't realise I'm hurt.
"I still can't understand why I was spared that night and why I'm still here."
"Obviously I was kept here for a reason — whether it's to go and speak at safety conventions and talk to people about how life is much better than it can be with the help of professionals.
"I get up every morning and thank my lucky stars I get to see another day."

On November 3, Russell took to social media to announce that "years of pain, uncertainty, appointments, treatments, setbacks, and endless battles plus the emotional exhaustion of having to pick myself up time and time again, have left me with nothing left to give".
"The time has come, medically and physically, where there are no further options on either front for me & there is no more fight left in me.
"I will leave hospital tomorrow after 8 and a half months for the last time to see out my days in my own home surrounded by my wife, kids, loved ones and friends.

"A massive thank you to the incredible staff at the Launceston General Hospital; their overwhelming support, care and kindness have helped to soften the daily grind of what has been an incredibly difficult journey."
Todd Russell is survived by his wife and children.
